title: Streaming QoS & Fallbacks: Launch Messaging and Enablement
content:
Executive summary:

Purpose: provide a compact, pragmatic messaging and enablement pack for the Streaming QoS + Fallbacks feature set (beta -> GA). Audience: field sales, solutions, Customer Success (CS), product marketing, and launch comms.

Why this matters (single sentence): Keep live conversational experiences responsive and predictable by automatically degrading gracefully when capacity or latency constraints occur — preventing user-visible stalls and preserving session continuity.

Key product elevator (2 lines):
- Keep the conversation flowing: streaming quality-of-service (QoS) and fallback policies ensure chat and streaming apps remain responsive even under contention.
- Works across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments with the same API and rollout controls.

Target customers / use cases:
- Fintech chat assistants where a single stalled reply is a critical UX failure.
- Customer support chat with SLA/response-time guarantees.
- Live collaborative editors and real-time summarization that must avoid token stalls.
- Startups scaling quickly who need to avoid engineering work to handle model degradations.

Customer-facing positioning bullets (short):
- Seamless fallback to compatible model variants or non-streaming mode when network, capacity, or GPU memory pressure would otherwise cause a stall.
- Configurable QoS tiers: conservative (prioritize latency), balanced, and high-fidelity (prioritize output quality).
- Observability hooks show per-request decision reasons (fallback trigger, selected variant, estimated latency) so customers can audit behavior.

Top benefits to lead with in comms:
- Reliability: reduces visible stalls and timeouts in chat UX by X-60% in internal tests (we need to finalize numbers).
- Predictability: customers can set latency SLOs and have automatic routing/fallbacks enforce them.
- Cost control: graceful fallback to smaller/quantized variants reduces per-token spend during contention.

One-line positioning statement for website header:
"Streaming that keeps up: graceful fallbacks and QoS controls to make LLM-powered live experiences reliable."

Competitive analysis notes (short-form, internal):
- Competitor A (LargeCloudModels): basic endpoint autoscale, no streaming-aware fallback. Pros: simple UX; Cons: when overloaded either drops requests or increases p99 dramatically.
- Competitor B (OpenRuntimeX): offers model variants but requires manual routing rules and complex infra; less polished telemetry.
- Comp C (Self-hosted vendors): flexible but customers own the whole complexity; strong for on-prem but high ops cost.

Redwood differentiators to emphasize in field / battlecards:
- Unified runtime: same API and policies across Hosted/Dedicated/Private (less friction moving from proof-of-concept to production).
- Smart routing + prefix/KV caching: fallbacks preserve continuity (reuse cached KV where possible) so degraded responses are still contextually coherent.
- Observability + causality: request-level explanation of fallback decisions in Console.

Sales battlecard snippet (how to win):
- Objection: "We can just run a smaller model ourselves."
  - Response: Sure — but the value is in turnkey signal-driven fallbacks, telemetry, and automatic KV-caching to preserve context without building orchestration or monitoring.
- Objection: "Fallback sounds like degraded UX."
  - Response: Fallbacks are policy-controlled (balance/latency/fidelity). In most cases we prefer multistage responses: start with streaming tokens from a smaller variant while asynchronously completing higher-fidelity output for subsequent messages.

Launch timeline (draft):
- Feb 12: internal alpha doc + initial eng PR (done).
- Feb 25: internal SRE + Console integration complete (monitoring flags).
- Mar 3: limited beta with 5 pilot customers (on Dedicated + Hosted).
- Mar 24: GA announcement and docs.
- Apr 7: enablement webinar and field playbook distribution.
(note: dates tentative — align with product/ops)

Enablement checklist (for GTM leads):
- Product one-pager written (this doc = working draft).
- Customer-facing FAQ and setup guide (docs/KB link) — owner: Lina (DOCS-67).
- Demo script and sample app that toggles QoS tiers — owner: Ethan (GH-1287).
- Slide deck for AE training (10–12 slides) — owner: Tomoko.
- Pricing guidance for fallback tiers and cost impact model — owner: Revenue Ops (need input).

Internal announcement draft (Slack/email) — short version (use for internal #product-launchs):
Title: "Beta: Streaming QoS + Fallbacks — keep live experiences responsive"
Body: "We’re rolling out a streaming QoS + fallback policy feature to reduce chat stalls and preserve session continuity. Starting Mar 3 we’ll invite 5 pilot customers; GA targeted for Mar 24. Key things for teams: Console will show per-request fallback reasons, API supports QoS param, and Dedicated customers can set policy at pool-level. Please read the alpha doc and add questions to the launch thread. — Maya"

Customer announcement draft (short) — email headline + 2 bullets:
Subject: "Redwood: Keep live chat responsive — new streaming fallback controls (beta)"
Lead: "Starting in beta, Redwood can automatically choose a lower-latency variant or non-streaming fallback when there’s resource contention — no code changes required. You control the QoS policy and see decision telemetry in the Console."
CTA: "Request access to the beta" with an Admin-only link (placeholder).

FAQ (working):
Q: Will fallback change response semantics?
A: Fallbacks prefer latency-preserving variants; we provide a confidence/variant tag in response and suggest customer-side heuristics for requerying high-fidelity model if needed.

Q: Can customers opt out?
A: Yes — default is ON for safety but customers can pin strict model version/no-fallback in Dedicated/Private.

Metrics to track (launch KPIs):
- Reduction in user-visible stalls (measured via APM traces + synthetic agent tests).
- Beta adoption (number of customers enabling QoS policies).
- Per-token cost delta during fallbacks (billing delta).
- Number of incidents attributed to fallback decisions (should be 0).

Open questions / unresolved items (action items):
- Finalize p95/p99 improvement numbers from eng perf tests (owner: Ravi, JIRA-RED-2987).
- Legal: any claim language we should avoid for SLA-related messaging? (owner: Legal).
- Pricing: how to surface fallback-related cost control vs. standard pricing (owner: RevOps).
- UX: Console text for "why fallback was chosen" — need copy review (owner: Product Writer).

Attachments / demos to ship with launch (notes):
- Demo app: chat UI showing graceful degrade -> streaming smaller model -> fallback metadata (GH-1287).
- Short video (1–2 mins) showing side-by-side: no-fallback stall vs. with-fallback smooth UX.
- A one-page cheat sheet for AEs that summarizes positioning, technical constraints, and demo steps.

Playbook snippets for CS / AE (quick):
- When to pitch: customers building chat, support, or live collaborative features; those with p95 latency sensitivity.
- Pilot ask: ask for a 2-week synthetic test span with our telemetry enabled to validate p99 improvements.
- Success criteria: visible drop in user-reported stalls + CSAT maintained or improved.

Notes to self / rough TODOs (very informal):
- Pull perf numbers from perf-run-20250207 (Ravi).
- Add sample curl + SDK snippet for QoS param to docs (Lina).
- Draft webinar script + figurehead (Tomoko + marketing).

References / links used while drafting:
- RED-Streaming-Fallbacks-Design (confluence)
- Git PR: runtime fallback heuristics (GH-1287)
- Internal perf run: perf-run-20250207

End of working draft.

-- Maya

(Comments welcome — particularly from Eng, SRE, Legal, and RevOps)
